content: Benzodiazepines (BZDs) are medications with sedative and hypnotic properties. While short-term use can be beneficial, long-term use is common and associated with significant risks, including the potential for dependence. This dependence can occur in both individuals with and without concurrent opiate dependence. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions in reducing harmful use, abuse, or dependence on BZDs. These interventions were compared to pharmacological treatments, no intervention, placebo, or other psychosocial approaches in both opiate-dependent and non-opiate-dependent populations. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and others, covering studies published up to December 2014. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated psychosocial interventions for BZD reduction. Data collection and analysis followed Cochrane methodological guidelines. A total of 25 studies involving 1,666 participants met the inclusion criteria. These studies examined various psychosocial interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) (with or without a tapering strategy), motivational interviewing (MI), patient-directed letters encouraging BZD reduction, relaxation techniques, electronic counseling, and advice from general practitioners (GPs). Two meta-analyses were conducted. The first compared CBT combined with tapering to tapering alone in 575 participants. The evidence was of moderate quality and showed that CBT plus tapering was more effective in achieving BZD discontinuation within four weeks post-treatment (Risk Ratio [RR] 1.40, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.05 to 1.86) and at three months post-treatment (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.98). However, the effects were less certain at longer follow-up intervals (6, 11, 12, 15, and 24 months). The evidence for CBT’s ability to reduce BZD use by more than 50% at any time point was of low quality. Additionally, the evidence regarding treatment dropouts at various time points was of very low quality. The second meta-analysis compared MI to treatment as usual (TAU) in 80 participants. The evidence was of very low quality, and the effects of MI on BZD reduction were unclear at all time points, including post-treatment (RR 4.43, 95% CI 0.16 to 125.35), three months (RR 3.46, 95% CI 0.53 to 22.45), six months (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.89), and 12 months (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.47). Similarly, the evidence for MI’s effect on reducing BZD use by more than 50% and on treatment dropouts was also very low quality. Other interventions showed some promise. A tailored GP letter was more effective than a generic GP letter at 12 months (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.70). A standardized interview was more effective than TAU at six months (RR 13.11, 95% CI 3.25 to 52.83) and 12 months (RR 4.97, 95% CI 2.23 to 11.11). Relaxation techniques were more effective than TAU at three months (RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.23 to 3.94). However, there was insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of other interventions. The quality of the included studies was assessed. High-quality evidence was found for random sequence generation, attrition bias, and reporting bias. Moderate-quality evidence was found for allocation concealment, performance bias for objective outcomes, and detection bias for objective outcomes. Low-quality evidence was found for performance bias and detection bias for subjective outcomes. Few studies used manualized intervention protocols or independently tested treatment fidelity, and most follow-up periods were less than 12 months. In conclusion, CBT combined with tapering is effective in reducing BZD use in the short term (up to three months). However, this effect is not sustained beyond six months. There is currently insufficient evidence to support the use of MI for BZD reduction. Emerging evidence suggests that tailored GP letters, standardized interviews, and relaxation techniques may be effective, but further research is needed. There is insufficient evidence to recommend other psychosocial approaches for reducing BZD use.
